title: Duolingo: Users Up 29%, Bookings Up 12%
topic: Turning a fast-growing free user base into paying subscribers without hurting the free product
hook: Duolingo's daily users grew 29% in a year, but bookings grew 12%. Management says 2027 leans into monetization. Which lever goes first?
tension: A much larger free base is a long-term asset only if it converts, yet pushing conversion too hard could damage the free experience that drives the growth.
disclosure: Educational case built from public company reports as of November 10, 2026. It is not investment advice, and the ratios in Exhibit 2 are our arithmetic, not figures the company reports.
brief: Duolingo reported third-quarter 2026 results on November 3, 2026. Daily active users reached 64.9M, up 29% from 50.5M a year earlier and faster than the 23% growth of the previous quarter. Paid subscribers reached 13.1M, up 14% from 11.5M. Total bookings, the money customers committed to spend in the quarter, were $316.1M, up 12% from $281.9M.

Users are growing faster than revenue. Subscription bookings rose 16% to $278.4M. Outside subscriptions the picture is weaker: advertising revenue was roughly flat at $20.8M, down 1%, and in-app purchase revenue fell 38% to $6.9M. Duolingo also accrued $11.4M in the quarter for a company-wide bonus tied to Q4 daily-user growth of 25% or greater.

Management says 2027 will lean more into monetization after a year focused on teaching quality and user growth, but with a firm internal rule not to make the free experience worse. It says a much larger active base is a long-term asset because some users take years to convert, and it gave no free-to-paid conversion rate. It also says paid subscriber growth is slowing and should bottom within a couple of quarters.

As of the November 3, 2026 call, the levers management has named are: longer free trials, which it says raise conversion and which it plans to expand; higher-quality advertising in place of low-quality ad networks, which it says will take time; in-app purchases such as avatar suits; Chess, which reached 10M daily users and which it calls under-monetized; a cheaper ad-supported tier, where tests have not been big wins; and the Family plan. Duolingo is also retiring its highest tier, Max, now a single-digit share of paid subscribers and bookings, because AI video calls that once cost about $0.30 each now cost under $0.01 and move into the Super tier.
Gross margin was 72.9% in the quarter. Duolingo guides to 72.0% for Q4 as video calls roll out to all paid subscribers.

question.text: You lead monetization planning for Duolingo's 2027 plan. Management says it will lean further into monetization but will not make the free experience worse. Choose the one lever you would scale first, and defend the choice with the numbers.

parts.label: Read the numbers
parts.prompt: What do the ratios say about the new daily users? Is the gap between user growth and bookings a problem, or a delay?

parts.label: Your lever
parts.prompt: Pick one lever from the brief, or propose another. Say who it targets, what you expect to change, and why it goes first.

parts.label: Test and guardrail
parts.prompt: What would you measure, what protects the free experience, and what result would make you stop?

parts.label: Biggest risk
parts.prompt: What is the most likely way this goes wrong, and what would you do about it?

rubric.name: Reading the data
rubric.measures: Whether the answer draws the right implication from user growth outpacing paid growth and bookings.
rubric.excellent: Notes that bookings per daily user fell, compares the two denominators (daily and monthly users) and explains why they differ, and says whether the gap looks like a delay or a leak and what would tell them apart.
rubric.weak: Restates the growth rates without saying what they imply, or declares the strategy a failure from one quarter.

rubric.name: Choice and sequencing of one lever
rubric.measures: Whether one lever is chosen and ranked against the others using the economics in the case.
rubric.excellent: Picks one lever, says who it targets and what should change, explains why it beats the others on the evidence, and says what would have to be true for another lever to win.
rubric.weak: Lists several levers without choosing, or picks one with no link to the numbers.

rubric.name: Use of the numbers
rubric.measures: Whether figures are used correctly across all parts, without inventing data.
rubric.excellent: Uses at least two figures correctly, labels derived ratios as ratios, and does not invent a conversion rate or any figure that is not in the case.
rubric.weak: Quotes a conversion rate the company has not disclosed, mixes up bookings and revenue, or misreads a ratio.

rubric.name: Test design and guardrail
rubric.measures: Whether the answer defines what is measured, how it is compared, and what protects the free experience.
rubric.excellent: A comparison group, a primary metric, a retention or growth guardrail for free users, and a clear stop condition.
rubric.weak: Says to run an A/B test and watch the results, with no metric, guardrail or stop condition.

rubric.name: Risk and second-order effects
rubric.measures: Whether the answer finds a plausible way the plan fails and responds to it.
rubric.excellent: A specific failure such as cannibalising existing payers or margin pressure, with a concrete response.
rubric.weak: A generic risk such as users may not like it, with no response.

model_answer.summary: Scale longer free trials first: they act on users already here, leave the free product alone, and management says they improve conversion. Test against a holdout with the daily-user growth goal as the guardrail.

parts.text: Daily users grew 29% while paid subscribers grew 14% and bookings 12%, so bookings per daily user fell 12.7% to $4.87. Paid subscribers as a share of daily users fell from 22.8% to 20.2%, yet against monthly users the share is flat, 8.5% to 8.6%. The two denominators disagree because the growth is in how often existing users show up, not in how many users exist. That reads as a delay, not a failure, since management says some users take years to convert. The risk is that part of the delay is permanent, which is why the response has to be tested.

Scale longer free trials. They target users who are already engaged, so they do not touch the free experience. Management says trials of video calls make people more likely to subscribe and that longer trials improved conversion. The other levers are weaker first moves: advertising revenue was roughly flat at $20.8M and the better ad mix will take time, in-app purchases are small and shrinking at $6.9M, the cheaper tier has not been a big win, and Chess is a separate product to build. Trials act on the 64.9M daily users immediately.

Run it as a holdout by country or cohort. Measure trial-to-paid conversion, retention after the first renewal, and bookings per new user against the holdout. The guardrail protects the free experience: daily-user growth must stay at or above the 25% the company has tied its bonus to, and free-user retention must not fall. Stop if bookings per new user do not beat the holdout once the cost of the trial, including AI usage, is counted.

Trial users cancel before paying, or existing payers wait for a trial instead of subscribing, and margin slips: Duolingo already guides to 72.0% for Q4, down from 72.9%, as video calls reach all paid subscribers. Cap the most AI-heavy features inside the trial and watch margin per trial user. If conversion rises but margin falls, shorten the trial for low-intent users.

alternatives.better_when: The goal is a new revenue line and conversion in the core app is already healthy.
Willingness to pay is low in the markets that drive growth, so reach matters more than subscriptions.

alternatives.option: Push the Family plan and tier pricing
alternatives.better_when: Conversion is healthy but revenue per payer is the gap.

common_traps.why: Duolingo has not disclosed one. Dividing paid subscribers by daily or monthly users gives a ratio, not a conversion rate, and the two denominators tell different stories: 22.8% to 20.2% against 8.5% to 8.6%.

common_traps.trap: Calling slower paid growth proof the strategy failed
common_traps.why: Management says users can take years to convert, so paid growth lags user growth by design. The better question is whether the gap is a delay or a leak.
A paywall on core lessons or other cuts to the free product contradicts management's stated rule and risks the daily-user growth that the company has tied a bonus to.
The task is to sequence. A strong answer says why one lever goes first and what would have to be true for another to win.

common_traps.trap: Treating the in-app purchase decline as the whole story
common_traps.why: In-app purchase revenue of $6.9M is small next to subscription bookings of $278.4M. It is a signal, not the lever to fix first.
